extracted.intended_audience: scholars of humor, comedy writers, and analysts of long-form humorous texts (e.g., novelists, sitcom writers, stand-up performers)
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying and evaluating the structural devices that distribute and sustain humor across extended texts (stories, novels, sitcom episodes, stand-up routines), using Attardo's constructs like jab lines, strands, stacks, combs, and the text vector.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punch line
rubrics_metrics.description: Text-final. Disrupts the narrative. The text ends or is heavily punctuated by it. The classical joke ends here.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to identify a concluding humorous resolution in short jokes or as a possible culminating moment in long texts; contrasts with jab lines. Look for a final disruption that terminates narrative continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jab line
rubrics_metrics.description: NOT text-final. Does not disrupt narrative flow — the story continues after it. Ontologically similar to a punch line (introduces a script opposition). Lives within the body of a longer text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary unit of humor in extended texts; long humorous texts contain many jab lines and may end with one major punch line. To annotate, mark in-text instances that introduce a script opposition but allow continuation of the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text vector (humor vector)
rubrics_metrics.description: The linear sequence of the text, segmented (e.g., into 100-word chunks). Plotting jab/punch line density across the vector reveals the humor topology of the text — where humor is concentrated, where it's sparse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize by segmenting the text and counting jab/punch lines per segment to find peak-density sections and sparse regions. Useful for comparing rhythm across works and for diagnostics (e.g., a 12,500-word story with 253 jab/punch lines had ≥3 peak sections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Strand
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence of related jab lines connected by topic, character, theme, or running gag. A strand can extend across many pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify recurring thematic/characterual loci where jab lines cluster; strands create continuity and expectation. Example: repeated jab lines about a character's idiosyncrasy form a strand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substrand
rubrics_metrics.description: A subdivision within a strand — narrower thematic continuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use substrands to capture finer-grained threads within a larger strand (e.g., a particular variant of a running gag). They help map nested or branching comedic motifs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central vs. peripheral strand
rubrics_metrics.description: Central strands are tied to the main plot and characters; peripheral strands are tangential threads — running gags, side characters, recurring imagery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify strands by their tie to the main narrative: central strands carry core comic weight, peripheral strands add texture. Evaluate interplay: central/peripheral balance affects perceived richness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stack
rubrics_metrics.description: A group of related strands that interconnect (multiple themes converging on a common comic territory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect when several strands overlap or feed into the same comic payoff; stacks show higher-level architectural convergence and can amplify payoff when coordinated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comb
rubrics_metrics.description: A strand with more than 3 jab lines occurring relatively close to one another in the text — a burst of comic density.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comb is a measurable burst: >3 related jab lines in proximate segments. Combs create concentrated humor and are important for rhythm and contrast with sparser stretches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributed jab lines (necessity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distributed jab lines — humor must occur regularly enough that the audience does not lose the comic frame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate frequency: too sparse and the audience may exit the comic frame; too dense without structure may fatigue. Aim for regular enough occurrences to sustain comedic engagement across the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Density variation (necessity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Density variation — combs (concentrated bursts) alternate with sparser sections to maintain rhythm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the alternation of high-density (combs) and low-density passages; effective pacing uses contrast between bursts and rests to maintain interest and maximize payoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strand coherence (necessity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Strand coherence — jab lines that belong to a strand reinforce each other (the audience anticipates the next instance, then enjoys the variation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge how consistently a strand repeats and how each instance varies; coherence builds expectation and reward, while incoherent repetition can feel aimless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strand termination or culmination (necessity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Strand termination or culmination — major strands often resolve in a punch line that integrates the running material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for integrative punch lines that pay off accumulated strand material; successful culmination binds dispersed jab lines into a satisfying payoff rather than merely concluding the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central/peripheral balance (necessity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Central / peripheral balance — the work has primary comic threads but is enriched by minor ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the ratio and interaction between primary strands and side strands; balanced mixtures prevent monotony and enrich texture without distracting from main threads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope limitation: exclusion of short/local humor
rubrics_metrics.description: What this excludes — Short jokes (covered by other models). Texts where humor is purely local and not structurally integrated are outside this architecture's domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Attardo's architecture only for long-form works where humor is structurally distributed; for single, isolated jokes apply short-joke models (SSTH, GTVH, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic questions for evaluating long humorous works
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of analytic prompts: What is the text's humor vector? Where are jab lines concentrated, where sparse? What are the major strands? Which are central, which peripheral? Are there combs and where? How does the work balance density and rest? Does the ending punch line integrate the strands, or merely conclude the narrative?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these questions as an evaluation checklist or annotation plan to map humor topology, identify strands/stacks/combs, assess pacing and culminations, and judge whether the architecture produces a coherent sustained comedic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequencing/ordering as an evaluative dimension
rubrics_metrics.description: The same set of jab lines can be funny or unfunny depending on how they're sequenced, which strands they belong to, and how density is distributed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or revising, consider not just individual jab-line quality but their order and placement within strands/stacks/comb patterns; set-order matters as much as joke quality in long-form comedy.
